title: Spectral Anisotropy in Transition Radiation from Biaxial Media
authors: Sven Ebel, Bibi Mary Francis, Min Seok Jang, Brian D. Gerardot, N. Asger Mortensen, Mauro Brotons-Gisbert, Sergii Morozov
abstract: In anisotropic optical media, the electromagnetic response depends on the orientation of the optical field relative to the material's principal dielectric axes. While this direction dependence is well understood in conventional optics, it should also influence light-generation processes driven by free electrons. Here, we experimentally observe spectrally anisotropic transition radiation from biaxial van der Waals crystals. Using cathodoluminescence spectroscopy on germanium sulphide (GeS) and molybdenum oxydichloride (MoOCl$_2$) crystals, we show that the transition-radiation spectra differ along the principal in-plane optical axes. To describe this spectral anisotropy, we develop a thin-film transition-radiation model that reproduces the experimental observations. Our results demonstrate that transition radiation is a sensitive probe of the axis-dependent dielectric response of biaxial optical media and suggest that optical anisotropy can provide an additional degree of freedom for free electron-driven spectroscopy, radiation sources, and transition-radiation-based diagnostics.
summary: This work reports on the experimental observation and theoretical modeling of spectral anisotropy in transition radiation emitted from biaxial van der Waals crystals. By rotating the sample and measuring polarization-resolved spectra, the authors prove that TR is highly sensitive to the material's orientation-dependent dielectric response. This opens up optical anisotropy as a new diagnostic tool for free electron-driven spectroscopy.
main_problem: The study investigates how the spectral anisotropy of transition radiation (TR) is influenced by the orientation-dependent dielectric response of biaxial optical media.
main_result: The authors experimentally demonstrate and theoretically model that TR spectra exhibit pronounced, measurable anisotropy when measured from biaxial crystals, confirming that TR is a sensitive probe of the material's optical axis dependence.
method: The research combines experimental cathodoluminescence (CL) spectroscopy, involving sample rotation and polarization-selective detection, with the development of a thin-film theoretical model.
model_or_system: The physical system involves biaxial van der Waals crystals (like GeS and MoOCl2) acting as the source. The model adapts the standard TR intensity formula to incorporate the two principal in-plane dielectric responses ($\varepsilon_{xx}$ and $\varepsilon_{yy}$) to predict orientation-dependent spectra.
key_observables: The primary observables are the polarization-resolved transition radiation spectra, measured as a function of the crystal's rotation angle ($\phi$) and the electron beam energy ($E$).
important_parameters: Key parameters include the crystal's principal dielectric axes, the electron beam energy (10–30 keV), and the orientation angle ($\phi$).
main_assumptions: The theoretical model uses an effective projection model to combine principal-axis intensities, which is noted as an approximation compared to a full vectorial treatment of the dielectric tensor.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the polarization-selective CL geometry, show angle-resolved spectra for isotropic materials (WS2), and demonstrate the periodic spectral changes and energy tunability for anisotropic materials (MoOCl2) along their principal axes.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical problem of anisotropy in TR, details the experimental setup using CL spectroscopy on biaxial crystals, develops an anisotropic thin-film model, and presents results showing the successful reproduction of angle-dependent spectra and energy shifts.
why_interesting: While the core physics is in condensed matter optics, the technique itself—using electron-beam induced radiation to map anisotropic dielectric tensors—is a powerful, non-destructive diagnostic tool applicable to characterizing complex quantum materials.
